c.tagline: Morocco's cosmopolitan port city of Art Deco boulevards and the soaring Hassan II Mosque.

taxi.fareNote: Small red 'petits taxis' (max 3 passengers) work within the city and are metered, but many drivers don't run the meter - insist on it or agree a price first, and expect to share the cab with other riders. Larger cream/white 'grands taxis' cover longer/airport trips at a negotiated flat rate.

emergency.note: Dial 19 for police and 15 for ambulance/fire; 112 also works from mobiles. Tourist police operate in the main visitor areas.

hood_landmark.Centre Ville: Boulevard Mohammed V and the Marche Central, Casablanca

avoid.reason: Petty crime; caution in the old medina and around the port at night

hood_desc: The dense, buzzing grid where Casablancans actually eat, drink, and shop - packed with restaurants, bakeries, cafes, and the Twin Center towers; the city's real social heart and better value than the tourist strip.

Casablanca's celebrated Art Deco and Mauresque district, with the highest concentration of 1920s-30s facades around Boulevard Mohammed V and Rue d'Alger; a walkable, leafy area loved by architecture fans.
The fashionable Corniche seafront strip lined with beach clubs, pools, trendy cafes, seafood restaurants and nightlife, a short hop from the Hassan II Mosque; best for beaches and going out.
The original walled settlement (once ancient Anfa), a small maze of narrow alleys, cheap eats and local life beside the port; atmospheric and central but rough around the edges, best explored by day.

Casablanca's downtown between Place des Nations Unies and Boulevard Mohammed V, the Art Deco core with the Marche Central, the tram lines and the widest choice of hotels at every price; central and well connected but busy and traffic-heavy.

water.note: City tap water is treated and usually fine, but most visitors and many locals drink bottled.

transit.hours: Trams run roughly 6am-11pm; city buses run from about 5:45am to 9:15pm, with no real night service.
transit.note: The modern Casa Tramway (4 lines) plus the newer Casa Busway rapid-bus lines are the easiest public transport for visitors; ordinary city buses cover the rest, while most short trips are done on foot or by red petit taxi.
transit.pay: Buy a rechargeable Casa Tramway card or a single-ride ticket at station machines - about 8 MAD (~US$0.80) per tram trip; city buses are about 4-5 MAD paid on board. Carry small change.

bus: Gare Routière Ouled Ziane (CTM / Supratours intercity)

transit.m: ONCF train from the airport station to Casa Port / Casa Voyageurs (~35-45 min, roughly hourly, 04:50-22:50)
Petit/grand taxi to the city center (30-40 min; agree the fare first)

tip.r: ~10% at sit-down restaurants if service isn't included; round up taxi fares and leave a few dirhams for cafe and hotel staff.

food.name: Tagine
food.desc: Slow-cooked in a conical clay pot: chicken with preserved lemon and olives, lamb with prunes and almonds, or the coastal fish and sardine-ball versions.

places.name: La Sqala
places.note: Inside an 18th-century bastion with a bougainvillea courtyard; tagines are well judged.

places.name: Al Mounia
places.note: Serving traditional Moroccan food in a garden of fountains and zellij since the 1960s.

places.name: Saveurs du Palais
places.note: Local favourite for tagines, including the sardine-ball version Casablanca does best.

food.name: Rfissa
food.desc: Chicken and lentils in a fenugreek and ras el hanout broth poured over shredded msemen. Traditionally cooked for new mothers and family feasts.

places.name: Dar Naji
places.note: Moroccan comfort-food house where rfissa and couscous are the point of going.

places.name: Al Mounia
places.note: Home-style dishes done properly in a formal setting; ask what the day's plat is.

places.name: La Sqala
places.note: Rotating traditional dishes beyond the tagines; call ahead to check for rfissa.

food.name: Grilled sardines
food.desc: Morocco lands more sardines than anywhere, and Casablanca eats them simply: salted and grilled over coals, or stuffed in pairs with chermoula and fried.

places.name: Marche Central
places.note: Buy from the fish stalls and the surrounding kitchens grill it while you wait.

places.name: Ain Diab corniche
places.note: Seafront strip of seafood grills; the heart of the city's fish eating.

places.name: La Sqala
places.note: Chermoula-marinated sardines in a courtyard setting rather than a market stall.

food.name: Msemen and harcha
food.desc: Breakfast breads: msemen is a flaky folded square griddled in butter, harcha a crumbly semolina cake. Eaten with honey, jam, amlou or soft cheese.

places.name: Bianca Cafe
places.note: Big terrace over the sea doing a full Moroccan breakfast with baghrir and msemen.

places.name: La Sqala
places.note: The city's best-known Moroccan breakfast: breads, olives, amlou and fresh juice.

places.name: Marche Central
places.note: Morning stands nearby sell msemen and harcha for a few dirhams each.

food.name: Couscous
food.desc: Steamed three times over a broth of seven vegetables with lamb or chicken, and eaten on Fridays after prayers. Many kitchens only make it that one day.

places.name: Al Mounia
places.note: Friday couscous is the thing to plan around; the garden makes a long lunch easy.

places.name: Dar Naji
places.note: Serves couscous beyond Friday, useful if your days do not line up.

places.name: La Sqala
places.note: Friday couscous in the fortress courtyard; go early, it sells out.

food.name: Bastilla
food.desc: Layers of warqa pastry over pigeon or chicken with almonds, egg and cinnamon, dusted with icing sugar. Sweet and savoury at once; seafood versions too.

places.name: La Sqala
places.note: The bastilla is one of the kitchen's signatures; order it to share as a starter.

places.name: Al Mounia
places.note: Classic almond and cinnamon version made to the old formal recipe.

places.name: Rick's Cafe
places.note: Film-set atmosphere with a competent Moroccan menu; book for the piano bar.

food.name: Mint tea
food.desc: Gunpowder green tea steeped with a fistful of spearmint and plenty of sugar, poured from a height into small glasses to build the foam. Never refuse a glass.

places.name: La Sqala
places.note: Poured the traditional way in the walled garden; the calmest tea stop in town.

places.name: Old Medina cafes
places.note: Street cafes near Bab Marrakech serve it all day for a handful of dirhams.

places.name: Al Mounia
places.note: Tea and Moroccan pastries in the garden after a long lunch.

food.name: Fresh juices
food.desc: Orange juice squeezed to order on nearly every corner, plus the thick avocado and almond shake, jus d'avocat, that Moroccans drink as an afternoon treat.

places.name: Marche Central
places.note: Juice counters press orange, pomegranate and avocado in front of you.

places.name: Bianca Cafe
places.note: The avocado and milk drink here is singled out by regulars as excellent.

places.name: Old Medina juice stalls
places.note: Cheapest orange juice in the city, squeezed while you stand at the counter.

landmarks: Hassan II Mosque
One of the world's largest mosques, its 210-meter minaret rises dramatically over the Atlantic Ocean, making it Casablanca's most photographed icon.
Casablanca Cathedral (Sacré-Cœur)
A striking Art Deco/Gothic former cathedral whose empty white shell and skeletal spires make for a hauntingly beautiful photo subject.
Rick's Café
A recreated version of the fictional bar from the film Casablanca, beloved by visitors for its old-world 1940s ambiance and cinematic legend.
Mohammed V Square
The elegant administrative heart of the city, ringed by French colonial-era buildings and a fountain that comes alive with light shows at night.
Twin Center
Casablanca's twin skyscraper towers form an unmistakable, ultra-modern silhouette on the city's skyline.
Habous Quarter (New Medina)
A charming 1930s-built 'new medina' blending traditional Moroccan architecture with colonial urban planning, ideal for photogenic archways and market scenes.
Corniche of Ain Diab
A lively seaside promenade lined with palm trees, beach clubs, and Atlantic Ocean views, perfect for sunset photography.
Old Medina
The city's original walled quarter offers narrow winding alleys, historic gates, and an authentic slice of pre-colonial Casablanca.
Morocco Mall
One of Africa's largest malls, famous for its giant aquarium and dancing fountain show set against the ocean.
Notre-Dame de Lourdes Church
A mid-century modern church renowned for its vibrant stained-glass windows designed by Gabriel Loire, a hidden gem for photographers.

train.note: No international trains - Morocco's network stops at the borders, and the Algerian frontier is closed. Casablanca is the hub of the country's rail system: Al Boraq high-speed trains reach Tangier in about 2h10 and Rabat in 50 minutes, while conventional services run to Marrakech in 2h30 and Fes in 3h30. Casa-Voyageurs is the main long-distance station; Casa-Port serves the centre and the airport shuttle. Book on the ONCF site or app for the cheaper advance fares.

intl.to: Spain, France, Belgium & Italy - road-and-ferry services

bus.note: CTM's international coaches cross the Strait of Gibraltar by ferry at Tanger Med and take a day or more to reach Spain and longer for France - carry your passport and check Schengen visa rules. Domestically CTM and Supratours (https://www.supratours.ma/) run from their own terminals rather than one central station, reaching Marrakech in 3-4 hours and Essaouira in 6.

ferry.note: Casablanca's port is Morocco's largest but handles containers rather than scheduled passengers - the old ferry to Europe no longer runs. All Morocco-Spain sailings leave from Tanger Med, Tangier or Nador in the north, or from Ceuta and Melilla. Take the train to Tangier and cross there.

half.name: Rabat
half.blurb: Morocco's capital, with the unfinished Hassan Tower minaret, the royal palace and the ancient walled Chellah necropolis gardens.

half.name: El Jadida
half.blurb: Fortified Portuguese coastal town with an eerie underground cistern and an atmospheric walled old city by the sea.

full.name: Marrakech
full.blurb: Red-walled imperial city with the Jemaa el-Fnaa night market square, maze-like souks and the Majorelle Garden.
